title: What is American Diamond (AD) jewellery
description: American Diamond or AD jewellery uses lab-made cubic zirconia. Learn what it is, how it compares to real diamonds, and how to keep AD sets sparkling.
intro: American Diamond, or AD, is the name Indian shops use for cubic zirconia, a colourless stone made in a lab. It is not a diamond and it does not come from America; the name is simply a trade term that stuck. AD is popular because it gives a bright, diamond-like sparkle at a small fraction of the cost, which makes it a favourite for receptions, cocktail nights and engagement functions.

sections.heading: What the stone actually is
paragraphs: Cubic zirconia, usually shortened to CZ, is a crystal grown from zirconium oxide under controlled conditions. Because it is made rather than mined, every stone can be cut cleanly and consistently, without the natural flaws you find in mined gems.

In India, 'AD' and 'CZ' are used almost interchangeably. Some sellers say AD for white stones and CZ for coloured ones, others use either word for everything. If a listing says AD, CZ or 'zircon stones', it is safe to assume you are looking at cubic zirconia, though you can always ask.

sections.heading: How AD compares with a real diamond
paragraphs: At a wedding, from a normal distance, a well-cut AD stone can easily pass for a diamond. Up close, there are differences worth knowing.
list: Sparkle: AD tends to throw more rainbow-coloured flashes than a diamond. Some people love this; others find it a little too lively.
Hardness: AD is hard enough for regular wear, but softer than diamond, so after years of use its edges can pick up tiny scratches and look slightly less crisp.
Weight: an AD stone feels a touch heavier than a diamond of the same size.
Cloudiness: AD can look dull when lotion, soap or skin oil builds up on the back. A gentle clean usually brings the shine back.
Value: AD has no resale value as a gem. You buy it for the look.

sections.heading: How AD jewellery is put together
paragraphs: Most AD necklaces, earrings and bangles have a base of brass or copper alloy. The stones are held in place by tiny metal claws (prong setting), packed close together in rows (pave or micro-pave), or occasionally glued into cups in cheaper pieces.

The base is then plated. White AD sets usually get a silver-tone or rhodium-style finish so the metal blends with the stones. Gold-tone and rose-gold finishes are popular too, especially when AD is mixed with coloured stones like emerald green or ruby red.
Prong-set and pave AD tends to look more expensive than glued AD because the stones sit higher and catch more light. It also holds up better, since claws do not weaken with moisture the way glue can.

sections.heading: Where AD works best in your wardrobe
paragraphs: AD shines, quite literally, under evening lights. It is the go-to for reception gowns, sarees in satin, organza or net, and Indo-western outfits. It also suits brides who want a lighter, more contemporary look than heavy gold-toned Kundan.

For a daytime haldi or mehendi, AD can feel too formal; Kundan, Meenakari or floral pieces usually suit those functions better. If you are curious about statement AD sets, Varaha's [Heritage collection](/heritage) has American Diamond necklace sets designed for exactly these evening occasions.

sections.heading: Signs of a well-made AD set
paragraphs: Two AD necklaces can look identical in a photo and feel completely different in hand. Before you buy, or as soon as a parcel arrives, check these points:
list: Every stone is the same whiteness. A few yellowish or greyish stones in a row of bright ones means mixed quality.
Stones are cut cleanly, with sharp, even facets that throw light when you tilt the piece.
Rows are straight and tightly packed, with no empty settings or visible glue.
Claws are small and neat, holding stones without covering too much of them.
The piece moves smoothly and lies flat on the neck, with no stiff or twisted joints.
The clasp or dori is sturdy enough for the weight of the set.

sections.heading: Keeping AD sparkling
paragraphs: The stones themselves are tough. The plating and the settings are what need care.
list: Spray perfume and set your hair before putting on the jewellery, not after.
After each wear, wipe the piece with a soft, dry microfiber cloth to remove skin oils.
To bring back shine, brush the stones gently with a dry, very soft brush such as a clean makeup brush. Avoid soaking, especially if the stones are glued.
Store each set in its own box or pouch so the stones do not scratch the plating of other pieces.
Check claws now and then. If a stone wobbles, stop wearing that piece until it is fixed.

faq.q: Is American Diamond a real diamond?
faq.a: No. American Diamond is the Indian trade name for cubic zirconia, a lab-made stone that looks similar to a diamond but is a different material.
The stones do not, but the plated metal can darken over time with moisture and sweat. Good storage and keeping it dry slow this down a lot.

faq.q: Is AD the same as CZ?
faq.a: In the Indian market, yes. Both terms usually mean cubic zirconia.

faq.q: Can a jeweller tell AD from diamond?
faq.a: Yes. A jeweller can quickly tell them apart with a simple diamond tester or a loupe.
